questions.question: Describe the four-sector circular flow: its participants, the markets in which they meet, and the two flows that run around it.
questions.expected_answer: The four participants are households, businesses, government and the foreign sector; the presence of the foreign sector is what makes the economy open rather than closed. Households own and supply the factors of production and receive wages, rent, interest and profit, which they consume, save and pay tax on. Businesses buy factor services, produce goods and services and undertake investment. Government taxes, spends and provides public goods; the foreign sector buys exports and supplies imports. They meet in four markets: the factor market, the product (goods and services) market, the financial market and the foreign exchange market. Two flows run in opposite directions: the real flow of factor services and of goods and services, and the money flow of incomes and expenditure facing it — every real flow has a money flow opposite it, which is why the diagram closes.

questions.question: State the equilibrium condition for the open economy, test it with the figures S = 300, T = 500, M = 400, I = 350, G = 550, X = 300 (R billions), and explain what happens if exports then fall to 250.
questions.expected_answer: Equilibrium requires total leakages to equal total injections: S + T + M = I + G + X. Leakages here are 300 + 500 + 400 = R1 200 billion and injections are 350 + 550 + 300 = R1 200 billion, so the economy is in equilibrium; note that the pairs need not match individually, only the totals. If exports fall to 250, injections drop to R1 150 billion against leakages of R1 200 billion. Stocks accumulate, firms cut production and retrench, incomes fall, and because incomes are lower, households save less, pay less tax and buy fewer imports, so leakages shrink. Equilibrium is restored, but at a lower level of national income with higher unemployment — the downswing described in circular-flow terms.

questions.question: Explain the three methods of measuring the flow and convert GDP at market prices of R6 000 billion into GDP at factor cost and into GNI, given taxes on products of R700 billion, subsidies on products of R100 billion, primary income received from abroad of R80 billion and primary income paid abroad of R200 billion.
questions.expected_answer: The flow can be measured at three points and must give the same total: the production method sums value added by every producer (value added, not total sales, so intermediate goods are not double-counted); the income method sums compensation of employees, net operating surplus and consumption of fixed capital; the expenditure method sums C + I + G + (X − M). GDP at factor cost = GDP at market prices − taxes on products + subsidies on products = 6 000 − 700 + 100 = R5 400 billion. GNI = GDP at market prices + primary income received from the rest of the world − primary income paid to the rest of the world = 6 000 + 80 − 200 = R5 880 billion. Because South Africa hosts more foreign-owned capital than South Africans own abroad, GNI structurally sits below GDP. Nominal figures must also be deflated to a base year before growth is judged, and compared with population growth before living standards are judged.
